impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting JMOL that patent claims directed to humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL invalidating Teva's headache patents covering humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies, reinstating the jury's findings of willful infringement and validity. The court found the specification's disclosure of prior-art methods for making and humanizing antibodies, combined with disclosure of one specific antibody, was sufficient to satisfy § 112. This decision has major implications for pharmaceutical patent scope in the biologics space.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for pharmaceutical companies with genus claims in the biologics and antibody space, affirming that disclosure of known methods and one species can support broader claims. Protects innovators' ability to secure broad patent coverage for biologic drug classes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar companies face greater difficulty challenging the validity of broad biologic patent claims, potentially delaying market entry for competing products.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and in striking the patent holder's damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the district court's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent against Intel on extraterritoriality grounds, while affirming on other grounds, and remanded for further proceedings. The court also addressed the propriety of striking damages expert theories for failure to disclose in contentions. This high-profile patent dispute between VLSI and Intel has significant implications for how extraterritoriality limits apply to method patents in the semiconductor industry.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from a more nuanced application of extraterritoriality doctrine, preserving infringement claims where steps occur domestically even in globally distributed manufacturing processes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global operations face continued uncertainty about when domestic use of patented methods triggers infringement liability, and must ensure thorough disclosure of damages theories in contentions.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court had sufficient evidence to estop Valve from asserting invalidity grounds under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) based on prior art references that were not raised in an earlier IPR petition.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel under § 315(e)(2), finding that the lower court relied on insufficient evidence to conclude that a skilled searcher reasonably could have discovered the prior art references at issue, and failed to adequately account for hindsight bias. The decision narrows the scope of IPR estoppel in district court patent litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from a higher evidentiary bar for patent holders seeking to invoke IPR estoppel, preserving additional invalidity defenses in district court litigation even after IPR proceedings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face a more difficult path to invoke IPR estoppel to limit invalidity challenges in district court, potentially increasing litigation costs and uncertainty.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages expert testimony and in reducing the jury's breach of contract damages award in a dispute over automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the reduction of breach of contract damages, reinstating the jury's original award. The case involved Ford's development of competing software while licensing Versata's automotive configuration tools under the MSSA.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors and trade secret owners benefit from expanded flexibility in presenting damages theories, including models measuring the defendant's enrichment in appropriate circumstances.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop in-house alternatives to licensed software face greater exposure to trade secret misappropriation damages, with courts required to consider broader range of damages methodologies.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before the plaintiff brought suit alleging misappropriation of medical device trade secrets through former employees.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL, holding that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred because the statute of limitations expired before suit was filed. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing. This decision vacated substantial damages and a permanent injunction against EOFlow for alleged misappropriation of insulin patch pump trade secrets through hired-away employees.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations, providing certainty about the outer bounds of liability exposure.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon learning of potential misappropriation; delay in filing suit risks losing DTSA claims entirely, even where misappropriation is proven on the merits.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the plaintiff presented legally sufficient evidence to establish that each of its four asserted trade secrets was protectable under California law, and whether a finding of inventorship based on generally known ideas could support patent invalidity.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding that the plaintiff failed to prove its asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known in the field. The court also reversed on patent invalidity, finding the alleged inventive contribution consisted of ideas that were generally known. The counterfeiting claim and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from rigorous scrutiny of whether asserted trade secrets actually derive independent economic value from not being generally known, raising the evidentiary bar for plaintiffs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners face heightened risk that courts will find their claimed secrets to be generally known information, particularly where the underlying concepts are widely discussed in the relevant industry.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2' to 'C1' in a chemical substituent definition between a provisional and non-provisional patent application constituted an obvious typographical error, thereby preserving the patent's priority date and avoiding anticipation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating Enanta's '953 patent covering coronavirus protease inhibitors, holding that the change from C2 to C1 in an alkyl group definition was not an obvious typographical error and thus the patent could not claim priority from the earlier provisional application. Pfizer's intervening public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (the active ingredient in Paxlovid) therefore anticipated the claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers and competitors benefit from strict application of priority rules, ensuring that patent scope cannot be retroactively expanded through claimed typographical corrections to cover intervening prior art.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders face significant risk from even minor discrepancies between provisional and non-provisional applications, which can destroy priority claims and render patents vulnerable to anticipation by intervening disclosures.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a weight-to-weight ratio limitation, and whether the court erred in waiving the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal of a preliminary injunction.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction blocking Hetero's generic competitor to Nuedexta, agreeing with the district court's claim construction of the weight-to-weight ratio limitation. However, the court vacated the district court's waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement, holding that a bond pending appeal is required. This decision preserves Otsuka's market exclusivity for its neurological drug through patent expiration.
impacts.positiveImplications: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies benefit from favorable claim construction supporting preliminary injunctions against generic entrants, preserving market exclusivity during litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies face barriers to market entry when preliminary injunctions are upheld, and brand companies must now post bonds pending appeal, creating financial accountability for erroneously obtained injunctions.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in denying JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents directed to non-uniform constellations in communication systems, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court also affirmed the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages. The decision provides important guidance on the Alice/Mayo framework for communications technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies defending against patent assertions benefit from continued judicial scrutiny of § 101 eligibility for communications patents, potentially narrowing enforceable patent scope.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the communications technology space face uncertainty about eligibility of claims directed to signal processing improvements, even after favorable jury verdicts on infringement and damages.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data via relay devices on farming equipment are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in declining to find the case exceptional under § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas, but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional under § 285. The court found the claims directed to conventional data collection, processing, and sharing activities implemented with generic computer components. The remand on exceptionality may result in attorney fee awards against the patent holder.
impacts.positiveImplications: Agricultural technology companies and other businesses defending against data-collection patent assertions benefit from continued invalidation of broadly-claimed data processing patents under § 101.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting data-collection and IoT-related patents face not only invalidity under § 101 but also potential exposure to attorney fee awards under § 285 if the case is found exceptional on remand.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) deposition testimony from a corporate representative who lacked personal knowledge of historical sales was admissible to establish the on-sale bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether software source code constitutes hearsay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible regardless of the witness's personal knowledge, and that computer source code commands are not hearsay statements. The decision clarifies evidentiary standards for proving prior art sales in patent invalidity challenges.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from broader admissibility of corporate representative testimony and source code evidence when proving on-sale bar defenses, even when original employees are no longer available.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater vulnerability to invalidity challenges based on historical prior art sales, as courts will accept 30(b)(6) testimony from representatives without personal knowledge of the relevant events.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner who grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue for infringement independently retains sufficient exclusionary rights to establish constitutional standing to bring an infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that patent owners who retain the right to independently sue for infringement possess a sufficient exclusionary right to satisfy Article III standing, even where substantial rights have been exclusively licensed. The decision clarifies the standing requirements for patent owners who have entered licensing agreements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners who license their patents while retaining litigation rights can confidently enforce their patents against infringers without joining their licensees, providing strategic flexibility in enforcement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential jurisdictional defense based on challenging a licensor's standing when the licensor has retained independent enforcement rights.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination of sensor-based logistics patent claims, and whether a non-party to underlying litigation may file IPR petitions on the statutory deadline of a party to that litigation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness finding and remanded for further proceedings, while declining to review the Board's denial of termination regarding Qualcomm's filing of IPR petitions challenging patents asserted against Roambee on Roambee's filing deadline despite Qualcomm not being a party to the underlying litigation. The decision raises important questions about potential abuse of the IPR system by third-party petitioners.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from closer scrutiny of PTAB obviousness analyses and potential limits on third parties filing IPR petitions as proxies for parties facing statutory deadlines.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that rely on third-party IPR filings as a strategic tool face uncertainty, though the court declined to directly address the propriety of such filings in this case.

impacts.caseName: Fuente Marketing Ltd. v. Vaporous Technologies, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a likelihood of confusion between a registered standard character 'X' trademark for cigars and a stylized X-with-dot mark for oral vaporizers.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the TTAB's dismissal of the trademark opposition, finding no likelihood of confusion between Fuente's standard character 'X' marks for cigars and Vaporous's stylized X-dot mark for vaporizers. Despite finding overlap in goods and trade channels, the Board's determination that the marks were sufficiently dissimilar was upheld. The decision provides guidance on likelihood of confusion analysis for single-letter marks across smoking-related product categories.
impacts.positiveImplications: New market entrants in adjacent product categories benefit from the recognition that even overlapping trade channels do not automatically create likelihood of confusion when marks are visually dissimilar.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trademark owners with single-letter marks may find it difficult to prevent registration of stylized variations in related product categories, potentially diluting brand exclusivity.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in using a single verdict form question covering infringement of all asserted patents, and whether certain building automation system patents are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments against ecobee, finding that the verdict form's single infringement question covering all four asserted patents was prejudicially defective. The court also remanded for further Alice step two analysis on the '495 patent while affirming eligibility of the '887 and '371 patents. The decision reinforces requirements for patent-specific verdict forms in multi-patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that jury verdict forms must separately address infringement of each asserted patent, preventing overbroad liability findings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in multi-patent cases face the burden of securing separate jury findings for each patent, increasing trial complexity and the risk of partial adverse outcomes on retrial.
